title: 8 Women
full_review:
Generations of leading French actresses gather under one murderous roof in the musical mystery comedy "8 Women" (Focus). It's a delightful, campy experience until the tone darkens considerably by the second half, capped off by a violent act that renders the film unpleasantly nihilistic.

The setting is Christmastime in a French countryside mansion of the 1950s. As the all-female cast is gradually introduced, patriarch Marcel is supposedly sleeping late upstairs. Alas, once everyone has arrived, Marcel is discovered dead in his bed, a knife in his back. With the phone lines cut and a snowstorm outside, the women are stranded, likely with a murderer in their midst. Each is suspect and each is hiding a compromising secret, soon to be revealed.

There's Marcel's chilly wife, Gaby (Catherine Deneuve), and her two daughters, the older and outgoing one (Virginie Ledoyen) and the younger and high-strung one (Ludivine Sagnier). Also living with them are Gaby's stingy mother (Danielle Darrieux) and Gaby's nasty sister (Isabelle Huppert). Last to arrive is Marcel's uninvited sister (Fanny Ardant). Rounding out the murder suspects are the domestics: the faithful housekeeper (Firmine Richard) and the saucy maid (Emmanuelle Beart).

Based on a 1960s play by Robert Thomas and directed by Francois Ozon, the film is a lush visual palette of exquisite costumes and coiffures as the fabled French actresses mix it up and occasionally burst into song. The lighting and cinematography offer a gorgeous veneer but the women are hollow. Once the whodunit intrigue devolves into catfights, the film happily winks at all the promiscuity and homosexuality that surfaces.

And so we are left with one-dimensional characters of no depth whose infidelities and cruelties are of no consequence as long as they continue to look glamorous. Genuine human love is dismissed, underlined by such songs as "There Is No Happy Love" and "We Are All Alone," and an absurdly gratuitous suicide is the graceless note that caps the empty proceedings.

Subtitles.

Due to sexual references and situations including lesbian kissing and a suicide, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
